leads.name: Rich Redmond
leads.post:
We are trading in our sea legs for long distance grandparenting! Priced to sell - she's been a wonderful cruiser.

1999 Cruisers Yacht 3375 Esprit - Negotiable
leads.flag: The only true transaction lead in this batch. He's actively selling, already listed it himself, and "Negotiable" in the headline signals he expects to haggle — which usually means he's unsure of the number. Exiting boating entirely, so no upgrade to sell him; the value here is helping him actually close.
leads.dm:
Rich — congratulations on the grandkids. That's the best reason there is to sell a boat.

One thing worth knowing on a 3375 at this age: the buyer pool is small but specific, and the ones who want an Esprit really want an Esprit. What kills those deals is almost never price — it's paperwork and survey surprises showing up late.

Two things that'll save you weeks if you haven't done them: get the title and any lien release in hand now, and pull together your service records on the 5.7s. Buyers at this price point get spooked easily, and a tidy folder does more for your number than dropping it another five grand.

Also — "Negotiable" in the headline invites lowballs before anyone's seen her. You might get better traffic with a real number and a line about what's been done recently.

Happy to tell you what 3375s have actually closed at lately if that'd help you set it. No catch, I just hate watching good boats sit.

leads.name: Wayne Rambo
leads.post:
2023 42 Cantius owner here. Purchased the boat used back in February. I have owned several bowriders and center consoles in the past, but not one with these Volvo IPS engines and pods.

The last two times out, when I started throttling up to cruise speed, I got an alert that the transmission filter was clogged, and had to throttle back… I have now replaced both oil filters on the transmissions…

I would like to check the transmission oil level, but apparently there is no dipstick on these D6-IPS500 drives… Anyone with a similar vessel with advice on where to find the transmission oil level reading?
leads.flag: Bought in February, first IPS boat, recurring alert that's cutting his outings short — and no dealer relationship yet. He's a recent buyer of a high-value boat who doesn't yet have a trusted person to call. That's a relationship opening, not a transaction.
leads.dm:
Wayne — congrats on the Cantius, and you're not missing anything obvious. There's no dipstick on the IPS drives; level is read through the EVC display, and the menu path moves around depending on which EVC generation and software version you're on. On a lot of 2023 boats that oil level page only populates if the sender is configured, which is why plenty of owners never find it.

More important than the menu, though: a clogged-filter alarm that only shows up as you come up on plane, right after you've changed both filters, is worth taking seriously before you chase the level. That pattern usually means one of three things — low oil, a suction-side restriction, or a pump starting to give up. Higher rpm demands more flow, so the fault shows up under load and clears when you back off.

The fastest way through this is a Volvo dealer plugging in VODIA and reading the stored codes. It'll tell you in ten minutes what you'd spend a season guessing at, and it logs the history in case something's under warranty.

Where are you keeping her? If you're anywhere near me I can point you at a Volvo tech who actually knows IPS rather than one who'll learn on your boat.

leads.name: Erick Calderon
leads.post: The boat is now 4 years old….the starboard and the port engines trim motors stopped working….is this a common occurrence? Any preventive measures?
leads.flag: Both trim motors failing at four years, and the ellipses read as frustration rather than curiosity. Owners who start questioning whether their boat's failures are "normal" are early in the process that ends with a listing. Worth answering well and remembering.
leads.dm:
Erick — both going at once is the useful clue here. Two motors don't usually fail simultaneously, so before you buy motors, check the relays and the harness connections.

Trim systems on most of these run through a pair of relays or a solenoid pack, and those sit somewhere that gets damp. Corrosion there takes out both sides at once and looks exactly like dead motors. Relays are a fraction of the cost, and it's a common misdiagnosis — plenty of people have bought motors they didn't need.

Quick check: when you hit the trim switch, do you hear a click from the relay area? Click but no movement points one direction; silence points another.

On prevention — it's mostly keeping water out of the connections. Dielectric grease on the plugs and making sure the drain paths near the pumps stay clear does most of the work.

Four years is early for this and I understand the frustration. It's usually not a sign of anything deeper.

leads.name: Jon Edenfield
leads.post:
YACHT SENSE module not detected???

New as 50 fly owner here. My yacht sense app was working however now when I touch the app, it says yacht sense module not detected.

Where is the yacht sense module located? I can't find it behind the helm… Is there some breaker or switch that needs to be on to activate it?

I do have two UPSs that I think may feed the network switch.
leads.flag: New owner of a 50 Fly, systems he hasn't learned yet, and he's guessing at his own electrical layout. Same profile as Wayne — recent buyer without a go-to person. Answer this well and he remembers who helped in week one.
leads.dm:
Jon — welcome to the 50. "Module not detected" is almost always a network or power issue rather than a dead module, especially if the app was working before.

Start with the network switch. YachtSense talks over the boat's ethernet network, and if the switch loses power the app sees nothing even though everything else looks fine. You mentioned two UPSs — worth confirming both are actually up and haven't dropped to bypass or run their batteries down. That alone explains a lot of these.

On location: it's typically in the main electrical distribution area rather than behind the helm — often in a locker or behind a removable panel near the DC panel. Layout varies by hull and year, so rather than pulling panels on a guess, your build's wiring diagram will show it. Azimut dealer support can send that over if you give them your HIN.

One thing before you go hunting: power the network switch down for a full thirty seconds and bring it back. A surprising share of these clear right there.

How's she running otherwise? First season with a new-to-you boat is always a list.

leads.name: Anthony Wicker
leads.post: On a 2001 2870 is it by design that if only the port motor is running, you have no steering, but if the starboard only or both motors are on then you have steering. My mechanic says there's only one steering mechanism. Is that true of most 2870s or is it just mine? My boat has two Penta 5.0 GI.
leads.flag: He's quietly checking his mechanic's answer against the crowd — which means trust is thin. Confirming what's normal and flagging what isn't builds credibility fast, and this one has a safety edge worth being careful about.
leads.dm:
Anthony — your mechanic is right that there's one steering system, not two. On twin sterndrive setups like yours the helm drives a single hydraulic circuit and the drives are tied together with a link bar, so both turn as a unit.

Where it gets specific to your boat is the power assist. The hydraulic pump is belt-driven off one engine — sounds like starboard in your case. Kill that engine and you lose assist, which is why steering feels dead with port only.

The part worth checking: losing assist should make the wheel very heavy, not make it stop working entirely. If you truly have no steering at all rather than just stiff steering, that's worth a closer look before your next trip — it points at something in the circuit rather than just the pump being off.

Easy test at the dock: starboard off, port running, and see whether the wheel moves the drives at all with real effort. Heavy but moving is normal. Nothing at all isn't.

Worth knowing either way, since it's exactly the situation you'd be in if that engine quit underway.

leads.name: Darcy Hughes
leads.post:
So the old, poorly manufactured, adjustment lever for the flybridge helm seat on my 2006 Azimut 55fly has failed. I purchased a replacement from Marine Max, but the lever casing is just a little too small to swap over so I'm trying to replace the whole slide rail mechanism. Unfortunately, it is glued down with what appears to be the same white stuff in all the seams of the superstructure.

Does anyone have any good tips or tricks on how to get this stainless steel slide unglued from the fiberglass tub?
leads.flag: Straight DIY question with no transaction behind it. Answering it well costs one message and earns standing in an Azimut owners' group, which is exactly the room worth being known in.
leads.dm:
Darcy — that white stuff is almost certainly a polyurethane adhesive sealant, 3M 5200 or a Sika equivalent. It's structural, which is why it's fighting you.

What works, roughly in order:

Heat first. A heat gun on low, worked slowly along the bond line, softens polyurethane a lot. Keep it moving so you don't scorch the gelcoat.

Then cut, don't pry. Braided fishing line or thin stainless wire sawed back and forth under the rail follows the bond line without gouging the tub. An oscillating tool with a long thin blade works too, but it's less forgiving — one slip and you're into fiberglass.

Chemical help if it's stubborn. A dedicated polyurethane debonder softens what heat won't. Give it time to work rather than forcing it.

What I'd avoid is levering against the fiberglass with anything rigid. The adhesive will usually win and take gelcoat with it when it lets go.

One thing while you're in there — check whether there's backing plate or coring under that tub. Worth knowing before you rebed the new rail.

leads.name: Benjamin Antonio Castro Rivera
leads.post:
We recently purchased a Yamaha 6 HP 4-stroke outboard for our inflatable tender. Since we often spend a couple of nights anchored in bays throughout the Caribbean, we use the tender quite a bit…

However, we haven't found a good permanent storage solution for the outboard while we're underway. We would prefer not to leave it mounted on the tender, and we're looking for a secure location or perhaps a custom bracket, mount, or rack somewhere on the boat.

Has anyone come up with a practical solution?
leads.flag: Cruising the Caribbean on a 38XO and solving a real problem. No transaction in it, but this is an engaged, active owner in a brand group — the kind of person whose recommendation carries weight later.
leads.dm:
Benjamin — the two setups that hold up are a rail-mount bracket on the aft rail or pushpit, or a padded chock in the lazarette with a strap.

Rail mount is more convenient day to day, but on a 6hp make sure the bracket is through-bolted with a backing plate rather than clamped. A 60-pound motor swinging on a rail in a beam sea will find any weakness you left it.

One thing worth checking before you settle on a position, since it catches people: Yamaha portables have a specified resting side, and laying it on the wrong one lets oil migrate into the cylinder. Your manual will show which. If you'd rather not think about it, store it upright on a bracket and the question disappears.

For the Caribbean specifically — a cover matters more than you'd expect. Salt spray on the powerhead while underway does more damage over a season than the running hours do.

What are you doing for a lifting solution? On a 38 that motor is right at the weight where a small davit or even a halyard-and-block setup starts being worth it, especially in any chop.
